references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says exactly the same thing: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.
Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners at Levi's house, which shows his fellowship with these groups and confirms the accusation made by his enemies against him.
Jesus explains that he has come to call sinners, not the righteous – this is the reason behind his association with tax collectors and sinners for which he was criticized.
The Pharisees and scribes grumble because Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them – the same type of accusation as in Luke 7:34.
When Jesus visited Zacchaeus, people grumbled and said that he had gone to be a guest at the house of a sinful man – a repetition of the accusation that he is a friend of tax collectors and sinners.
Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners in Matthew's house, and the Pharisees ask his disciples why their teacher does this.
The proverbial warning against being among drunkards and gluttons – the background for the accusation made against Jesus as a 'glutton and a drunkard'.
The Mosaic law concerning the rebellious son who is a glutton and a drunkard – the serious background for the accusation made against Jesus, implying lawbreaking deserving of death.
The previous verse contrasts John the Baptist, who neither ate bread nor drank wine, and was called demon-possessed – a contrast to the accusations against Jesus in verse 34.
Isaiah describes shepherds who are glad with wine and strong drink – similar language about excessive drinking used in the accusation against Jesus.
Jesus calls himself 'the Son of Man' – a messianic title also used here in Luke 7:34 when he describes himself.
Daniel's vision of the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven – the background for Jesus' use of the title 'Son of Man' in this verse.
